strengths: Rigorous mathematical framework with formal theorems and proofs establishing approximation guarantees for symmetric representations (Theorem 3.3 with error bound in Eq. 83)
Novel and comprehensive treatment of all 17 planar symmetry groups through affine reflection groups and Hiroraka decomposition, providing theoretical foundations previously unavailable
Versatile framework demonstrated across three distinct design tasks plus metamaterial generation, showing broad applicability
Clear experimental improvements in maintaining strict symmetry (Figure 5 shows CLIP-A scores consistently outperforming baselines) with comprehensive comparisons
Well-motivated solution to the fundamental problem of preserving both symmetry and continuity in 2D representations, with clear exposition of why naive approaches fail (Figure 2)
Honest treatment of limitations and thorough technical appendices establishing conditions for existence of higher reflectional symmetries (Theorems B.9-B.13)
Zero-shot metamaterial generation capability demonstrates that explicit symmetry-specific training data is unnecessary
weaknesses: Dense presentation with heavy mathematical notation creates accessibility barriers; key intuitions (e.g., importance of Hiroraka decomposition) should be explained before formal treatment rather than assuming reader familiarity

Significant gap between theoretical guarantees (L_2 error bounds in Theorem 3.3) and practical claims of 'perceptually perfect' symmetry preservation; connection between theorem error and image quality not established
Limited to 2D patterns with unclear path to 3D extension, reducing long-term impact given recent advances in 3D symmetry-aware generation
Practical improvements over simpler baselines sometimes marginal—Table 1 shows narrow gap between method and basis projection at higher basis fractions; Figure 7 topology results show modest gains
Insufficient guidance on when the complex mathematical machinery is necessary versus when simpler symmetrization suffices; paper doesn't provide clear criteria for practitioners
Evaluation primarily compares against conditional generation + post-hoc symmetrization rather than other symmetry-aware methods; limited baseline diversity
Computational complexity never discussed despite involving Fourier decomposition and Reynolds averaging; runtime and resource requirements absent from main text

strengths: Rigorous mathematical framework using Hiroraka decomposition to systematically construct symmetric continuous representations for all 17 planar symmetry groups
Comprehensive theoretical treatment of crystallographic groups with careful handling of edge cases (non-symmetric groups, higher dimensions) in extensive appendices
Demonstrates practical versatility across diverse applications (visual pattern design, paper-cutting, topology optimization, metamaterial design) using a unified framework
Achieves zero-shot symmetric generation without requiring symmetry-specific training data
Well-developed mathematical exposition with detailed proofs establishing approximation guarantees
weaknesses: Limited machine learning novelty: the core contribution is mathematical (group theory application) rather than algorithmic. The ML component amounts to applying existing Score Distillation Sampling with additional loss terms

Insufficient experimental validation: only compares against general MLLMs and simple baselines; no comparison with other symmetry-enforcement techniques. No statistical analysis, error bars, or significance testing provided

Presentation issues: extremely dense mathematical exposition with weak motivation connecting abstract theory (Sections 3-4) to practical generation (Section 5). Inaccessible to readers outside crystallography/group theory specialization
Limited experimental scope: only 17 planar groups demonstrated; no evidence of generalization to 3D, frieze groups, or other symmetry classes. No perceptual user studies validating design quality

Unclear practical necessity of theoretical complexity: the approximation guarantees in Theorem 3.3 apply existing theory; it is unclear whether designs actually benefit from these theoretical guarantees versus simpler symmetry-enforcement methods
Missing ablations and analysis: no sensitivity analysis for loss term weights, no comparison of basis projection baseline rigor, no computational complexity discussion or runtime analysis

Disconnect between components: the topology and metamaterial design sections feel disconnected from the core symmetric representation framework and introduce standard domain-specific losses without clear integration

strengths: Strong mathematical foundation with rigorous theorems on affine reflection groups and Hironaka decomposition, providing theoretical guarantees for symmetric representations
Versatile framework demonstrated across four distinct domains (pattern design, paper-cutting, topology optimization, metamaterial design) without requiring domain-specific symmetric training data
Impressive zero-shot capability for metamaterial design, generating structures with prescribed symmetries without symmetric training examples
Comprehensive experimental validation with detailed comparisons against multiple baselines and thorough ablation studies
Excellent presentation quality with clear visualizations (all 17 planar groups, detailed comparisons in Figures 11-16) and meticulous implementation details enabling reproducibility
Novel problem formulation solving the practical challenge of enforcing exact symmetries in continuous representations
weaknesses: Modest practical improvements in some experiments (pattern design: 4.30 vs 4.05 CLIP-A; Table 1) suggesting incremental gains despite strong theoretical framework
Limited ML novelty - core contribution is applying established group theory to existing generative models (diffusion, SDS loss) rather than developing new algorithmic techniques
Incomplete exploration of continuous vs. discrete representation trade-offs mentioned in Section A.2 but not thoroughly investigated empirically
Heavy mathematical notation and dense presentation may limit accessibility to broader ICML community; Algorithm 1 is minimal and doesn't fully capture algorithmic contributions
Experimental scope could be broader - applications somewhat specialized (patterns, paper-cutting); stronger baselines and more diverse tasks would strengthen claims
Limited discussion of failure modes, computational costs, computational complexity analysis, and when symmetry enforcement is inappropriate or helpful

strengths: Rigorous mathematical framework using Hirónaka decomposition and crystallographic group theory with properly stated theorems and proofs for handling all 17 planar groups systematically
Comprehensive and unified treatment of symmetric pattern generation across three complementary applications (visual design, paper-cutting, topology design) demonstrating broad applicability
Well-structured presentation of complex mathematical concepts with helpful examples and clear figure illustrations of generated patterns across all planar symmetry groups
Theoretically sound approximation guarantees (Theorem C.12) for decomposing arbitrary invariant functions and precise mathematical formulation of affine reflection groups and secondary invariants
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: The heavy mathematical framework (30 pages of appendices) has unclear connection to the actual generative pipeline. Algorithm 1 is overly simple; it's unclear how the parametrized representation θ is jointly optimized with diffusion models or how low-symmetry bases from Theorem C.9 are instantiated in practice

Empirical results are modest and sometimes contradictory: Figure 5 shows CLIP-A scores degrade with stricter symmetry enforcement (e.g., p1mg: 3.2→3.1), suggesting the symmetry constraints reduce aesthetic quality. Post-symmetrization (Fig. 3) is required, undermining the theoretical contribution

Severely limited experimental validation: (1) No user studies validating preference for symmetric outputs; (2) No comparison with other symmetry methods (SymmCD, basis projection only in appendix); (3) Different prompts used for different methods (Appendix F.1.2), confounding results; (4) CLIP-A metric not justified for design tasks requiring manufacturability/structural properties

Reproducibility concerns: (1) Code availability stated but no link provided; (2) Relies on proprietary models (GPT-5.2, Gemini); (3) Paper-cutting dataset is Chinese designs only; (4) No systematic ablation studies on loss weights or architectural choices; (5) Computational costs and training times unspecified

Post-symmetrization requirement (Fig. 3) directly contradicts the core claim that continuous representations enforce symmetry. If refinement is necessary, the theoretical guarantees don't hold in practice, raising fundamental questions about the approach's validity

Dense and inaccessible presentation: Main method contributions buried in 30-page appendix with heavy mathematics. Inconsistent notation (G ambiguity). Connection between §3.2 (decomposition) and §5 (loss functions) is unclear. Missing practical details (group specification workflow, sensitivity analysis)

Multiple loss functions (SDS, VTM, connectivity, mechanical constraints in §5) without clear explanation of weighting, interaction, or how they preserve theoretical symmetry guarantees. No analysis of conflicting gradient directions or convergence properties

Limited scope and generalization: (1) Only 2D planar groups—no 3D crystallographic groups or frieze patterns; (2) Three specialized applications with unclear real-world necessity; (3) Visual quality in Figs. 11-12 appears noisier than baselines despite claimed superiority; (4) No discussion of failure cases

strengths: Rigorous mathematical framework: Combines group theory and representation theory with formal proofs (Theorems 3.2, 3.3, B.6-B.7, C.9), providing solid theoretical foundations for the symmetrization approach
Addresses real problem effectively: First systematic framework to incorporate exact planar group symmetry into continuous generative models without boundary discontinuities
Multi-domain applicability: Demonstrates effectiveness across pattern design, paper-cutting, topology design, and metamaterial design without requiring retraining, showing genuine generalizability
Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple visual design tasks, quantitative metrics (CLIP-A scores, bulk modulus, mechanical properties), qualitative results, and comparisons with baselines
Practical utility demonstrated: Generated designs are manufacturable as verified through paper-cutting examples; results show strong symmetry preservation
Thorough presentation: Well-organized main paper with clear motivation, excellent figures, and comprehensive appendices containing full mathematical derivations and experimental details
Reproducibility: Code made available with detailed hyperparameter specifications and optimization procedures clearly described
Novel unified approach: First work to apply symmetry constraints across diverse design domains in a single framework
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Primarily applies classical group-theoretic results (Hirorioka decomposition) rather than introducing new computational methods
Theory-practice gap: Approximation guarantees are asymptotic (Theorem 3.3); visual inspection of results reveals minor asymmetries suggesting gaps between theory and implementation

Incomplete evaluation: Lacks user studies validating design quality and aesthetic preferences; CLIP-A scores are indirect measures of symmetry preservation; no manufacturing feedback from actual paper-cutting production
Missing computational analysis: No discussion of computational cost of symmetrization versus unconstrained generation; scalability concerns unclear

Scope limitations: Focuses only on 2D planar groups (not 3D space groups); requires pre-specification of target symmetry group; pattern design still relies on imperfect diffusion model outputs requiring post-correction
Weak quantitative symmetry metrics: Relies primarily on visual inspection rather than quantitative measures of symmetry preservation error
Limited baselines: Comparisons mainly against single recent work (Zhong et al. 2023); few comparisons with other symmetry-enforcement approaches
Insufficient discussion of failure modes: Limited analysis of when approximations may be poor or when the method struggles
